n: Abraham takes another wife, Keturah. Whether this happened after Sarah’s death or earlier is not clear; 1 Chronicles calls her a concubine.

f.g: Her name may mean “incense.”

n: Keturah bears six sons, ancestors of Arabian desert tribes. Most notable is Midian, ancestor of the Midianites.

f.g: The Midianites included Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, from whom Moses received the priesthood.

n: Jokshan’s descendants include Sheba and Dedan, names of Arabian trading peoples.
Midian’s sons are listed. Ephah later appears as a people known for camels and trade.
Abraham leaves his entire estate to Isaac, the covenant heir.
Abraham gives gifts to his other sons and sends them east, away from Isaac, so there would be no dispute over the inheritance. He provides for all his children.

f.g: Secondary wives—here Hagar and Keturah.
The lands east of Canaan, toward Arabia.

n: Abraham lives 175 years—a full century after he first left Haran.

f.w: an hundred threescore and fifteen years
f.g: 175 years (a “score” is twenty).

n: Abraham dies peacefully, satisfied with life, and is “gathered to his people.” This phrase suggests joining his ancestors beyond death, hinting at life after death.

f.g: Breathed his last; died. “Ghost” means spirit.

n: Isaac and Ishmael bury their father together. Abraham’s death brings his estranged sons together.

f.g: A touching reunion of half-brothers.

n: Abraham is buried with Sarah in the field he bought—his only owned piece of the promised land.

f.w: there was Abraham buried, and Sarah his wife

n: God blesses Isaac after Abraham’s death. The covenant passes to the next generation.
Before following Isaac, Genesis briefly records Ishmael’s family, showing that God kept His promise to him too.
Ishmael’s sons are named. Nebajoth and Kedar became well-known Arabian tribes.

f.g: A powerful Arabian tribe often mentioned by the prophets (Isaiah 21:16; Psalms 120:5).

n: More of Ishmael’s sons, linked with oases and regions of Arabia.

f.g: Perhaps the oasis of Dumat al-Jandal in northern Arabia.

n: The list continues, completing twelve sons.

f.g: An important oasis in northwestern Arabia (Job 6:19).

n: Ishmael has twelve sons who become tribal princes, just as God promised—a parallel to Jacob’s twelve sons.

f.g: Encampments or fortified settlements.

n: Ishmael lives 137 years and dies, joining his ancestors.
Ishmael’s descendants spread across the desert between Egypt and Mesopotamia, living alongside—and sometimes in tension with—their relatives, just as foretold.

f.w: in the presence of all his brethren

f.g: The desert region near Egypt’s eastern border.

n: Isaac’s family story now begins.

f.g: A new major section of Genesis begins (toledot).

n: Isaac married Rebekah at forty. She came from Paddan-aram, “the plain of Aram,” in northern Mesopotamia.

f.g: The region around Haran in northern Mesopotamia.
An Aramean.

n: Like Sarah, Rebekah cannot have children. Isaac prays earnestly for her, and the Lord answers. The covenant line repeatedly depends on God’s miracles, not human strength.

f.g: Prayed earnestly; pleaded.

n: The twins struggle within her, and Rebekah, troubled, goes to ask the Lord herself. She seeks personal revelation.

f.g: Literally “why this, I?”—an expression of distress.

f.w: she went to inquire of the LORD

n: The Lord reveals to Rebekah that two nations are in her womb and that the elder will serve the younger. This revelation shapes her later actions.

f.w: the elder shall serve the younger

f.g: Israel (from Jacob) and Edom (from Esau).

n: When the time comes, she gives birth to twins.

f.w: her days to be delivered were fulfilled
f.g: Her time to give birth arrived.

n: The first baby is red and covered with hair, so they name him Esau. These details anticipate his later names and homeland.

f.g: Hebrew ’admoni—a wordplay on Edom (“red”).
Hebrew seʿar—a wordplay on Seir, Edom’s mountain homeland.

n: The second baby comes out gripping his brother’s heel, so he is named Jacob. Isaac is sixty when the twins are born—twenty years after his marriage.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew ʿaqev, “heel”; it can mean “he grasps the heel” or “he supplants.”
Sixty.

n: The twins grow into very different men: Esau an outdoorsman and skilled hunter, Jacob a quiet man who stays near the tents.

f.g: Skillful.
Hebrew tam—quiet, settled, even “whole” or “blameless”; the same word used of Job.

n: Isaac favors Esau for the game he brings home; Rebekah favors Jacob. Parental favoritism plants seeds of conflict.

f.g: Wild game, not just deer.

n: Jacob is cooking stew when Esau comes in from the field, exhausted and starving.

f.g: Boiled; cooked.
A thick soup or stew.
Exhausted; weak with hunger.

n: Esau demands some of the “red stuff.” His coarse words reveal his appetite, and earn him the nickname Edom, “red.”

f.g: Literally “that red, that red stuff”—Esau seems too hungry even to name it.
Means “red.”

n: Jacob seizes the moment to ask for Esau’s birthright—the firstborn’s rights of leadership and a double inheritance.

f.g: The firstborn son’s privileges: leadership of the family and a double portion of inheritance.

n: Esau exaggerates his need and shrugs off the birthright as useless. He values a meal more than his spiritual heritage.

f.w: what profit shall this birthright do to me?
f.g: “What good is a birthright to me?”

n: Jacob insists that Esau swear an oath, and Esau sells the birthright.

f.g: An oath made the transfer binding.

n: Esau eats, drinks, gets up, and leaves—four quick verbs that show his careless attitude. The narrator concludes that Esau “despised” his birthright. Hebrews uses him as a warning against trading eternal blessings for momentary desires.

f.g: Lentils.
